question: Quote VERBATIM with exact Pasal number: does any primary Indonesian immigration regulation (Permenkumham 22/2023, Permenkumham 11/2024, Permenimipas 5/2025, UU 63/2024) set a 5-year minimum stay/residence figure as an ALTERNATIVE eligibility route for ITAS-to-KITAP conversion -- for example for investor KITAP-INV or retiree KITAP-RET categories under Pasal 173, or any category distinct from Pasal 179(1)'s 3-year rule? Is there a second article, separate from Pasal 179(1), that sets 5 years for any KITAP-eligible category? Cite article number, quoted text, and source ID for every claim. If no such 5-year eligibility article exists anywhere in NB-2's primary sources, state that explicitly.
answer:
No primary Indonesian immigration regulation within the current framework (**Permenkumham No. 22/2023**, **Permenkumham No. 11/2024**, **Permenimipas No. 5/2025**, or **UU No. 63/2024**) sets a **5-year minimum stay/residence requirement** as an eligibility or alternative route for alih status (conversion) from ITAS (temporary stay permit) to KITAP (permanent stay permit) [1-3]. 

Under the current operative framework, **there is no second article in these regulations that sets a 5-year stay requirement for any KITAP-eligible category.** Instead, they establish a uniform **3-year requirement** under Pasal 179 [1].

The precise normative breakdown, verbatim quotes, statutory tensions, and distinctions between national and Balinese local rules are detailed below.

---

### 1. The Operative Rule: Uniform 3-Year Requirement (Pasal 179)
Under **Permenkumham No. 22 Tahun 2023** (as amended by **Permenkumham No. 11 Tahun 2024**), the required continuous stay in Indonesia to qualify for an ITAS-to-KITAP alih status conversion for workers, religious workers, investors, and retirees is strictly **3 years**, not 5 [1, 4].

The sole governing article is **Pasal 179 ayat (1)**, quoted verbatim below [1]:

> **Pasal 179 ayat (1) [Verbatim Bahasa Indonesia]:**
> *"Alih status Izin Tinggal Terbatas menjadi Izin Tinggal Tetap bagi Orang Asing sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 173 huruf a, huruf b, huruf c, dan huruf f diberikan dengan ketentuan Orang Asing yang bersangkutan telah berada di Wilayah Indonesia paling singkat 3 (tiga) tahun berturut-turut sejak tanggal diberikannya Izin Tinggal Terbatas."* [1]

**Official English Translation:**
> *"Change of status from Limited Stay Permit to Permanent Stay Permit for Foreigners as referred to in Pasal 173 letter a, letter b, letter c, and letter f is granted on the condition that the Foreigner concerned has been in the Territory of Indonesia for at least 3 (three) consecutive years since the date the Limited Stay Permit was granted."* [1]

The referenced categories under **Pasal 173** are [4, 5]:
*   **Huruf a:** *sebagai pekerja* (workers, such as TKA E23) [4, 6].
*   **Huruf b:** *sebagai rohaniwan* (religious workers under E27) [4, 7].
*   **Huruf c:** *penanaman modal asing* (foreign investors, such as standard E28A or Golden Visa E28B/E28C/E28G) [4, 8].
*   **Huruf f:** *rumah second home* (which includes second home property/deposit holders, specialized experts, world figures, and retirees/lansia aged 55 or older) [4].

#### Immediate and Marriage-Based Conversion Rules
For context, the only other categories defined for ITAS-to-KITAP alih status are governed by **Pasal 179 ayat (2) and (3)**, neither of which mentions a 5-year stay [1, 9]:
*   **Pasal 179 ayat (2):** Family reunification (*penyatuan keluarga* - Pasal 173 d) and repatriation (*repatriasi* - Pasal 173 e) can convert **immediately** (*dapat dilaksanakan sejak Orang Asing yang bersangkutan diberikan Izin Tinggal Terbatas*) [1].
*   **Pasal 179 ayat (3):** Spouses of Indonesian Citizens (WNI) are subject to a **2-year marriage validity requirement** (*perkawinannya yang sah dan resmi telah mencapai paling singkat 2 (dua) tahun*), rather than a minimum physical stay duration [9].

---

### 2. The Statutory Tension: The Origin of the "5-Year" Stay Requirement
If the current ministerial regulations (Permenkumham 22/2023 and 11/2024) enforce a **3-year** rule [1], why do secondary guidelines in your notebook (such as `nb2_golden_visa.txt` [10], `nb2_visa_procedures_guide.txt` [11], and `izin_kerja_tka_procedura_completa_2025.txt` [12]) mention a **5-year** stay?

This stems from a **statutory-regulatory conflict** within the Indonesian legal hierarchy:
*   **The Foundational Law (UU No. 6 Tahun 2011 on Immigration):** **Pasal 60 ayat (1)** of this primary national law explicitly dictates a **5-year** minimum consecutive stay requirement:
    > *“Alih status Izin Tinggal Terbatas menjadi Izin Tinggal Tetap bagi Orang Asing sebagaimana dimaksud dalam Pasal 54 ayat (1) huruf a diberikan dengan ketentuan Orang Asing yang bersangkutan telah berada di Wilayah Indonesia paling singkat 5 (lima) tahun berturut-turut sejak tanggal diberikannya Izin Tinggal Terbatas.”*
*   **The Ministerial Overhaul (Permenkumham 22/2023):** When the Ministry of Law and Human Rights overhauled the system, they operationally lowered this threshold to **3 years** under **Pasal 179 ayat (1)** to attract foreign capital and talent [1, 13]. 
*   **Subsequent Reforms:** Neither **UU No. 63 Tahun 2024** (the Third Amendment to UU 6/2011) [14] nor **Permenimipas No. 5/2025** (which specifically addresses guarantor/penjamin rules) [15] contains any articles reinstating the 5-year stay statutory rule. 

As an immigration specialist, I must note that while the operational portals (Molina/SIAPKerja) and Kantor Imigrasi currently process applications based on the **3-year ministerial regulation**, the underlying statutory law (UU 6/2011) technically still references 5 years, creating a classic Indonesian administrative-legal discrepancy that is frequently highlighted in operational briefs [10, 11].

---

### 3. Other Occurrences of "5 Years" in Primary Regulations
To ensure absolute legal precision, there are indeed articles in **Permenkumham No. 22/2023** that contain the figure of **5 (lima) tahun**, but they refer to stay validity, reporting intervals, or retirement ITAS limits, and are completely separate from alih status eligibility:

1.  **ITAP Stay Validity — Pasal 121 ayat (1):**
    > *"Izin Tinggal Tetap diberikan untuk jangka waktu 5 (lima) tahun."*
    > *(Permanent Stay Permits are granted for a duration of 5 years.)* [16]
2.  **ITAP Reporting Intervals — Pasal 132 ayat (1):**
    > *"Orang Asing pemegang Izin Tinggal Tetap dengan jangka waktu tidak terbatas wajib melapor setiap 5 (lima) tahun sekali kepada Kepala Kantor Imigrasi..."*
    > *(Foreigners holding unlimited ITAPs must report once every 5 years.)* [17]
3.  **Golden Visa Stay Validity — Pasal 185 ayat (2):**
    > *"Visa tinggal terbatas, Izin Tinggal Terbatas, Izin Tinggal Tetap dan Izin Masuk Kembali sebagaimana dimaksud pada ayat (1) diberikan untuk jangka waktu paling lama: a. 5 (lima) tahun; atau..."* [18]
4.  **Retirement ITAS Sabbatical — Pasal 62 ayat (1):**
    > *"Permohonan Visa tinggal terbatas bagi Orang Asing lanjut usia... yang akan tinggal tanpa Penjamin paling lama 5 (lima) tahun..."* [19]

---

### 4. National Rules vs. Bali Local Regulations
It is critical to distinguish national-level immigration structures from local Bali administrative rules:
*   **National Stay Permits (National Jurisdiction):** Rules regarding stay permit durations, alih status conversions, indices (such as E23 or E28) [20, 21], and stay requirements are strictly **national law**. No Balinese local regulation (*Peraturan Daerah*) can alter the 3-year alih status limit or override Kemenimipas regulations [1, 6].
*   **Bali Local Rules (Provincial/Regional Jurisdiction):** Local Bali regulations focus strictly on regional taxes and civil surveillance. This includes the **Rp 150,000 Bali Tourist Levy** under **Perda Bali No. 2/2025** (which replaced Perda No. 6/2023) [22] and the operational enforcement on the ground. For instance, Bali's **"Dharma Dewata"** patrol task force and local **TIMPORA** (foreign surveillance committees) monitor social media and local establishments to ensure foreigners holding stay permits are not engaging in unauthorized local work or barter [23], but they enforce the transition requirements strictly under national ministerial guidelines [24].
